title: After You Die, What's Left Isn't the Cause of Death — It's the Version of You Other People Assemble
dek: All three stories do the same thing: once a person is dead, the people left behind can only reconstruct someone who can no longer speak from fragments — texts, obituaries, Facebook comments — and the version they piece together often bears no resemblance to how the person saw themselves.
why: A narrative show, no data or mechanisms, but each of the three stories has a twist, and the second story's twist is the most valuable. Medium information density, good for the commute.
who: Listeners who like narrative podcasts and are interested in death and the stories told after someone dies; people working in hospice care, psychological crisis intervention, or grief counseling will find it especially resonant.
skip: Act One, Nadia's long letter, runs nearly 25 minutes and is the slowest stretch; if you're short on time, jump straight from 29:44 to Act Two.

points.h: After you die, other people will get you wrong
points.body: As a kid, Graham was playing on a seesaw at a construction site and dropped a 25-pound curbstone from second-story height, trying to launch a brick off the other end. The brick didn't fly — it shot straight at his face and grazed past his hair. He survived, but decades later what he keeps thinking about isn't the terror of that second. It's something else: if the brick had actually killed him, how would a coroner have read the scene? A brick, a seesaw, a kid — could they have pieced together the truth? That's where the show states its thesis for the whole episode — death itself isn't the hardest part; the hard part is the judgment other people make about who you were after you're gone.

points.h: She has now outlived her sister
points.body: Nadia wrote a long letter to the drug dealer who killed her sister. The sharpest cut in it isn't anger — it's arithmetic: at 6:49 p.m. on March 11, 2018, she outlived her sister's age. She had spent a few more seconds in this world than the sister who was two and a half years older. She says it makes no sense, that he bent the universe crooked. She went through her sister's phone, read the texts, listened to the voicemails, trying to figure out the life her sister had finally refused to share with her. She even admits she needs this dealer: because of him, she can say "if it weren't for that person," and she doesn't have to hate her sister, or herself.

points.h: The message she never answered became the last one
points.body: A few days before her sister died, her sister sent an offhand text asking if she remembered the little stick-figure illustration labeled faible (weak) in their middle-school French textbook. It was an old joke between the sisters. Nadia was still angry about their last fight and deliberately didn't reply, wanting to punish her a little. But a strong thought surfaced: you don't want this to be the last message she ever sends you. She still didn't reply. After her sister died, she found a text her sister had sent a friend that same night: "How do I stop hating my sister? My family really hates me." The friend replied: "Damn, Nadia the snitch." When she saw the word "hate" sitting next to her own name, she felt hollowed out.

points.h: He lived to read his own eulogies
points.body: Comedian Dave Marr was in a diabetic coma for a month. His friends thought he was going to be taken off life support; more than fifty people gathered at his house for a vigil, and 1,700 Facebook friends started writing eulogies on his wall. Then his parents didn't pull the tube, he was transferred to another hospital, and he woke up. During recovery, in his parents' basement, he read from 2 a.m. to 3:30 a.m., getting through about a hundred eulogies. He read his brother's post trying to set the record straight, buried by the algorithm with only 70 likes, while the posts mourning him got double the likes. He read someone remembering how he'd kicked in a storage-room door at a party insisting it was the bathroom, read an ex-girlfriend thanking him for breaking up with her in the car because it was cold outside, read someone saying he "sweats unreasonably much."

points.h: The man in the eulogies is a stranger to him
points.body: After reading all the eulogies, Dave wasn't moved — he felt bad. The self he remembers is someone who shoplifted at Walgreens and spent a night in jail; the self in the eulogies is known by every Walgreens clerk, buys people free Chipotle, treats everyone as an equal. He says it's hard to square the image in his own head with the image people described when they thought he was dead. He insists the coma was his own doing — "it was my carelessness, my recklessness that got me here." Blake's side is a different story: he lost a friend and got him back, and now Dave's laugh is like music to him. The show says both men got a second chance, to love and to be loved, and the latter is much harder than the former.

Retired Navy officer Charlie went to the funeral of a stranger, a SEAL named Eddie Furlani, in place of a friend. He couldn't find any reporting on the cause of death and assumed it was a training accident. At the funeral he noticed the back rows packed with big men in three-piece suits and sunglasses, expressionless the whole time, until Eddie's seven-year-old daughter Zelma broke down crying and was taken out by her stepmother. After the service he called his friend to report back, and the friend said, "I'm glad someone came, I was worried no one would," then added, "because of the way he killed himself." Charlie says that moment was like grabbing a live wire — no reporting, no mention in the obituary, not a word in the eulogy.

points.h: The daughter was crying because she felt ashamed
points.body: The day before the interview, Charlie called Eddie's widow to confirm, and only then learned that Zelma had cried and asked to leave the funeral not out of grief but out of shame — she thought everyone knew her dad had killed himself, and that she was a bad person. Charlie says hearing this terrified him: a seven-year-old girl treating herself as an outcast because of her father's death, when the room was full of people who had come to support her. He also talks about veterans losing their "larger mission" after they leave the service, and says he can probably put himself in Eddie's shoes and understand what he was thinking in that moment — but when asked whether he could say more, he stops, saying he can't take on that subject.

points.h: He wanted to be the sound of that helicopter
points.body: Charlie has had suicidal thoughts himself; this ended his Navy career, and he only agreed to talk about it after the mic was off. The host asks whether he wrote the piece because Eddie's funeral could be his own future funeral, and he says no. He explains the real reason: on medevac flights he knew that the sound of the helicopter approaching alone could improve a dying person's vital signs. He says, I'm writing to you because I want to be that helicopter sound for someone. The show ends with the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, 800-273-TALK.

terms.def: A conscious awareness of one's own death; the title of Act Two, "Comento Mori," is a punning rewrite of it.
A mission using helicopters and the like to move wounded personnel from the battlefield to a medical point; Charlie flew these in Iraq.

quotes.text: Your own death, that is not bad enough on its own. There's the whole question of the forensics afterwards, what people will make of it.
You don't want that to be the last text she ever sends you. Read the subtext. She may need you, and you need to let her know that you love her.
Why should my comfort be that there would have been another one, that all we can expect from life is a game of whack-a-mole but with shitty people?
I remember shoplifting from Walgreens and spending the night in jail. That's how I remember this stuff.
It's just really tough to square the image that I have of myself with the way other people talked about me when they thought I was dead.
The military trains you to separate the emotion from the mission. Eddie's oldest girl, Zelma, was old enough to understand what was happening, but not military enough to know not to show it.
I wrote you because I wanted to be the sound of a helicopter to someone.
